title: Recording the meaning of a keepsake without oversharing
description: The meaning of a keepsake can be explained without sharing every personal detail.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: The meaning of a keepsake can be explained without sharing every personal detail. Include only the context needed to understand what should be preserved or represented.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Write a private note about why the object matters, then make a shorter version for the atelier. Identify which details affect arrangement or personalization. Mark any names, dates or stories that must not appear publicly. Keep publication permission separate from the making discussion.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “These flowers mark an important family occasion” may explain the intention without identifying the people, venue or exact date.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which public-use decision has not been made?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A request to discuss preservation is not permission to publish the object or its story. Suitability still depends on the item and its condition.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: A condition note before discussing preservation
description: A condition note creates a shared description before preservation is discussed.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A condition note creates a shared description before preservation is discussed. It should record what you can observe without diagnosing causes or promising treatment.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Photograph the whole item and relevant details without unnecessary handling. Note visible changes, loose parts and any known prior treatment. Date the note and distinguish first-hand observations from information supplied by someone else. Keep the original item with you until guidance is provided.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: “Several petals appear curled at the edge” is an observation. A claim about why they curled or how they will respond to preservation requires appropriate expertise.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What should be discussed before handling or transfer?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not clean, repair, dry or alter an irreplaceable item based on an editorial reference. Ask for item-specific guidance.

title: Selecting photographs that explain a sentimental object
description: Keepsake photographs should explain identity, condition and priorities without exposing unnecessary private information.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Keepsake photographs should explain identity, condition and priorities without exposing unnecessary private information. A useful set has different purposes for its images.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Begin with a whole-item view. Add details that show the features you want retained and any concern about condition. Number the images to match an item list. Avoid placing personal documents or identifying background details in the frame.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A close-up may explain why a small ribbon matters, while the whole view shows its relationship to the flowers. Both are useful for different reasons.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What private background information can be removed?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Photographs do not establish suitability or guarantee a preservation result. Wait for guidance before sending originals.

title: Keeping a list of items and their priorities
description: An item list helps distinguish what is essential from what is optional in a keepsake discussion.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An item list helps distinguish what is essential from what is optional in a keepsake discussion. It also prevents several small objects from being treated as one undefined bundle.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Assign each item a simple reference, description and priority. Record whether it is irreplaceable and whether inclusion is a request or an open question. Match photographs to the references. Keep any transfer inventory separate from the first design list.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A flower, ribbon and note may carry different meanings. The brief can prioritise the flower while asking whether the other items are suitable to include.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does every photograph match the list?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Listing an item does not confirm it can be preserved or safely transported. Those decisions require specific guidance.

title: Discussing visible arrangement before handing over materials
description: An arrangement discussion can begin before original materials are handed over.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An arrangement discussion can begin before original materials are handed over. This allows the visual intention to be explained while suitability remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Use labelled photographs or simple paper shapes to compare arrangements. Mark which parts are approximate and which relationships matter. Record whether orientation, spacing or a particular detail is the priority. Ask what can be assessed from the references and what needs closer review.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A centred flower arrangement and an off-centre arrangement may express different priorities. Comparing them on paper does not require moving fragile originals repeatedly.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which arrangement question can be discussed now?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A layout reference cannot guarantee the final appearance or the survival of a particular material. Keep originals until current transfer guidance is confirmed.

title: Questions to resolve before transporting keepsakes
description: Transporting a keepsake should follow specific guidance, not an assumption based on an address found online.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Transporting a keepsake should follow specific guidance, not an assumption based on an address found online. Resolve the recipient and arrangements before anything leaves your care.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Prepare an item list and condition photographs. Ask about suitability, the current recipient, destination and transfer method for those particular items. Record the instructions and any unresolved responsibilities. Keep the discussion linked to the existing inquiry when one exists.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A general delivery address does not necessarily establish how a fragile sentimental item should be sent. The transfer discussion needs to concern the actual item.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which transfer question is still open?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This worksheet supplies no packing or transport instructions. Follow the atelier's current item-specific guidance and do not send irreplaceable originals prematurely.

title: Distinguishing an arrangement reference from a preservation promise
description: An arrangement reference communicates a visual intention, while a preservation promise would claim a result.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An arrangement reference communicates a visual intention, while a preservation promise would claim a result. Keep those two ideas separate in the brief.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Describe the desired orientation, spacing and emphasis. Label generated or illustrative images clearly. List the original materials being considered and their known condition. Ask which aspects can be assessed before any final design is agreed.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A clear floral block illustration may show a preferred composition. It does not prove that the reader's flowers can retain the same colour, form or arrangement.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What result does it not establish?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Never infer preservation suitability, permanence or exact appearance from an image. Those are questions for the actual materials and proposal.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Planning which names and dates may appear publicly
description: Names and dates used in a private commission do not automatically belong in a public story.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Names and dates used in a private commission do not automatically belong in a public story. Decide these permissions separately and explicitly.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: List each identifying detail and its intended use: private brief, object personalization or possible public caption. Record who can authorize each use. Keep unresolved public uses marked as pending. Review image backgrounds as well as written captions for accidental disclosure.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A date may be required on the object while the family prefers it omitted from website photographs. That distinction should be recorded before a public image is selected.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Which may appear on the object?
Which public use has actual permission?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not assume that agreeing to personalization grants permission for marketing or public attribution.

title: A consent checklist for a memory-art project story
description: A memory-art story needs permission for the particular text and images being shared.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A memory-art story needs permission for the particular text and images being shared. A broad assumption of consent is not enough to describe a private occasion publicly.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Prepare a proposed public caption and image list. Identify names, dates, locations and recognisable people in each. Record the allowed attribution and usage for the exact material. Keep the permission source private and link it to the reviewed version.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Permission to show an object without a name may not cover a longer family story. Treat those as different publication choices.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Who has approved which use and version?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This is a planning checklist, not legal advice or a claim that permission has been obtained. Unapproved stories stay unpublished.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Reviewing a preservation brief with family members
description: Family members may value different aspects of the same keepsake.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Family members may value different aspects of the same keepsake. A shared review helps preserve those differences before a design is treated as agreed.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Ask each participant to identify one essential meaning and one arrangement preference. Compare these against the same item photographs. Separate emotional priorities from assumptions about what preservation can achieve. Record unresolved choices and who will communicate the consolidated brief.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: One person may value a flower's position while another wants the original grouping recognised. The brief can state both before asking what is possible.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What needs a shared decision before the next conversation?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A family discussion does not establish material suitability or consent from absent participants. Keep those decisions open until addressed.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.
